html:
The hundreds of thousands of handwritten books kept for centuries in family libraries in Timbuktu, Mali, and in nearby towns. In 2012 and 2013 most of them were smuggled to safety from armed Islamist groups.

Timbuktu grew rich on the trade across the Sahara, and under the Mali and Songhai empires it became a centre of Islamic learning. Scholars taught at its mosques, and books were among the most valued goods brought by caravan.

Most of the manuscripts are in Arabic; some write African languages such as Songhay and Fulfulde in Arabic letters. They cover Islamic law and theology, but also astronomy, medicine, mathematics, poetry, letters, trade records and the history of the region. Many were written or collected by scholars such as Ahmad Baba. Families kept them hidden through invasions and colonial rule.

In 2012 rebels and jihadist groups took northern Mali in the Mali War. Librarians led by Abdel Kader Haidara packed the books in metal trunks and moved them secretly by car and boat to Bamako. When the militants fled in 2013 they burned some manuscripts, but the great majority survived.
sum: The hundreds of thousands of handwritten books kept for centuries in family libraries in Timbuktu, Mali, and in nearby towns. In 2012 and 2013 most of them were smuggled to safety from armed Islamist groups.
